claim: Israel never wanted a Palestinian state; or, the Palestinians rejected every offer.

heard.who: Marwan Barghouti, Palestinian leader, in The Guardian, 2015
heard.quote: The real problem is that Israel has chosen occupation over peace, and used negotiations as a smokescreen to advance its colonial project.

heard.who: Elliott Abrams, Council on Foreign Relations blog, on Abbas's 2015 interview
heard.quote: Abbas walked away, just as Yasser Arafat had walked away at Camp David in 2000.

answer: Both slogans are too simple. The Zionist leadership accepted the principle of partition in 1937 and the Jewish community accepted it in 1947; the Arab leadership rejected both. At Khartoum in 1967 Arab states said no peace, no recognition, no negotiations, yet in 2002 the Arab League offered normal relations for full withdrawal, and Israel did not accept that as a basis for talks. Oslo set up self-government and did not promise a state. In 2000 Clinton said both leaders accepted his parameters with reservations; Ross says Barak's were within them and Arafat's were not, while Malley and Agha say the proposals were never fixed offers. In 2008 Olmert showed Abbas a map; Abbas did not sign and later said he rejected it. In 2020 Netanyahu agreed to negotiate on Trump's plan; Abbas rejected it. Our reading: refusals came from both sides, at different moments.

contested: The strongest case that Israel never wanted a state: Oslo's text did not promise one while, by one scholarly count, the settler population grew from 115,000 in 1993 to 200,000 in 2000; Sharon's government never accepted the 2002 Arab offer as a basis for talks; and Malley and Agha argue that Barak's Camp David ideas were conditional, unwritten and never mapped, so there was no offer for Arafat to accept. Avi Shlaim writes that building settlements 'does not violate the letter of the Oslo accords but it most decidedly violates its spirit'.

The strongest case that the Palestinians rejected every offer: the Arab leadership rejected the 1937 and 1947 partitions, the Khartoum summit refused negotiation, Dennis Ross argues that Arafat's reply to the December 2000 parameters was a 'no', and Abbas told Israeli television in 2015 about the 2008 offer: 'I rejected it out of hand.' Elliott Abrams reads that as proof that Israel's version of events is correct.

Whether Zionist acceptance of partition was principled or tactical. The UN's own history says the 1937 Congress judged it 'too early' to accept a state in only part of Palestine, because the ultimate aim was a Jewish state in all of it; Khalidi reads Peel as satisfying Zionist aims at the Palestinians' expense, including the transfer of about 200,000 Arabs (OSU figure). Defenders reply that the Congress and the Jewish community in 1947 accepted a plan that left an Arab state beside Israel.

How much land Peel gave the Jewish state: the Ohio State history says 17 percent of the country, the UN study says about a third of the area; the sources define the area differently and the card does not choose between them.

How large Olmert's offer was: the BBC film shows 4.9 percent of the West Bank annexed to Israel; in the Associated Press interview Olmert speaks of Israel keeping 6.3 percent, in return for land swaps. Whether Abbas rejected the offer (his 2015 words) or was not given time to study it (his explanation, and Olmert's account that a meeting of map experts was agreed and never held) is disputed.
could_not_verify: Taba 2001, the Road Map of 2003 (including Israel's reservations to it), and the Kerry talks of 2013-14: not covered here because we did not read three reliable pages for each; the Road Map text itself is on Avalon but we did not find a reliable page on each side's response.

The full text of the Arab Peace Initiative as a readable HTML page: the UN copy we found is a PDF, so the terms rest on CBS News and the Council on Foreign Relations; Elie Podeh's article on Israel's non-response could not be read.
Abbas's 2009 statement to the Washington Post that 'the gaps were wide' (the page would not load for us).

Fewer than three reliable sources: the 1947 responses (one UN page plus two government pages), the Peel recommendation (two reliable plus an advocacy site), Khartoum (Avalon and The Guardian only), Resolution 242 (Avalon and the UN only, plus a government page), the Arab Peace Initiative (CBS and CFR, plus an advocacy-labelled think tank). The Olmert fact leans on a CFR blog post by a partisan author for Abbas's 2015 words.
Barak's Camp David percentages from a primary document: Malley and Agha say no written offer exists. The Peel report and Dennis Ross's book were not read directly.

A reliable third source for the 1947 acceptance and rejection: the UN page and two US government pages carry it, but Britannica could not be read by our fetcher and Khalidi's text has no plain statement.
not_claimed: Listing who refused what does not by itself assign blame: a refusal can be reasonable, forced by politics, or a mistake, and the card does not rank the refusals.
It does not claim any of these plans would have produced peace, or that Barak's and Olmert's offers were signed texts.
It does not claim Zionist acceptance in 1937 or 1947 was unconditional or sincere, or that Arab refusals were unjustified.
It does not claim Abbas or Arafat spoke for every Palestinian, or that Israel's governments always spoke for every Israeli.
It does not say that the Arab Peace Initiative was an offer Israel should have accepted as written.
